citation: Baroni DB, Franz-Montan M, Cogo K, Berto LA, Volpato MC, Novaes PD, Groppo FC. Effect of articaine on mental nerve anterior portion: histological analysis in rats. Acta Odontol Scand 2013;71(1):82-87 (epub 29 Mar 2012)
text_quality: ok (6 PDF pages, published version; micro, degree and multiplication signs dropped in extraction; 'Mental nerve' is printed 'Metal nerve' in the figure labels; Figures 3-8 are qualitative photomicrographs, Figure 2 repeats Table I)
design: Controlled animal experiment, split-mouth (injected right side vs saline-injected left side of the same rat), three parallel groups, qualitative histopathology; Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn tests
population: Healthy male Wistar rats, 60 days old
n: 24 rats, 8 per group: articaine with epinephrine (G1), lidocaine with epinephrine (G2), epinephrine alone (G3); every rat also had a contralateral saline control side
setting: Laboratory, Piracicaba Dental School, University of Campinas (UNICAMP), Brazil; animal ethics protocol CEEA-Unicamp #830-1
intervention: One injection under thiopental anaesthesia into the alveolar mucosa beside the lower right first molar, near the mental nerve (Figure 1) - not into the nerve: G1 articaine with epinephrine, G2 lidocaine with epinephrine, G3 epinephrine alone, each at the standard marketed dental formulation (the paper gives volumes and concentrations on PDF p3; not repeated here). Only one articaine concentration was tested.
comparator: Saline injected into the contralateral mucosa of every rat; comparisons between the three groups
route: Submucosal infiltration beside the mental nerve in the rat mandible (extraneural); not intraneural, not intradermal
duration: Single injection; one time point - animals killed 24 h after injection
outcomes: H&E light microscopy of serial sections where the mental nerve crosses the cortical bone: qualitative 1-5 score of leucocyte (inflammatory) infiltration in the soft tissue and nerve near the injection site, and presence of necrosis. No nerve morphometry or stereology, no electrophysiology, no sensory or behavioural testing, no later time point.

key_results.quote: The rats were divided into three groups (n = 8).
The previous described solutions ([dose figure omitted]) were injected in the alveolar mucosa close to the lowerright first molar of rats (Figure 1)
After 24 h, the animals were killed and the samples (mandible and the soft tissue adhered) were removed.
The images were submitted to qualitative analysis in order to evaluate the intensity of leucocytes infiltration and/or any possible necrosis area.

An inflammatory infiltration was found around mental nerve, classified as intense for G3, moderate for G1 and light for both G2 and control groups. No injuries were found in nervous structure, despite the inflammatory reaction observed around it.

The mental nerve was not histologically affected by the treatments. However, higher scores (p < 0.05) of inflammation in connective tissue were observed when epinephrine was administered alone (Group 3) than associated with the local anesthetics (Groups 1 and 2).

Similarly, in the present study no significant increase in score inflammation was observed 24 h after articaine injection. Microscopic analysis of nervous structure showed no difference between the treated and the control sides.
Similarly, the present study demonstrated that lidocaine was similar to saline solution and less toxic then articaine, although no statistical difference was observed.
Despite the intense inflammation observed in this group, there was no evidence of injury to the nervous structure.
So, it was suggested that an important cause of paresthesia could be related to the local anesthetic dosedependent neurotoxicity. Some in vitro studies support this hypothesis [27,28].

Although the higher incidence of paresthesia associated to the use of [dose figure omitted] articaine formulation in comparison to other local anesthetics [10–13], the hypothesis that this local anesthetic may be neurotoxic was not confirmed in the present study.

The results of the present study suggest that articaine is not toxic to the nervous structure and that further studies are necessary to explain the possible relation between articaine injection and paresthesia.

less toxic then articaine, although no statistical difference was observed
